title: About Common Cold

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: A cold is a viral infection of the upper respiratory tract (also called an upper respiratory infection or URI). Colds usually last less than a week and are caused by different respiratory viruses. They are also one of the most frequent reasons for missed school and work. Every year in the United States, adults have an average of two to three colds, and children often have more.

sections.heading: Mild to moderate:
sections.text: Middle ear infections (infection behind the ear drum)

sections.heading: Potentially severe:
sections.text: Worsening of chronic medical conditions (for example, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, heart failure)

sections.heading: Causes
sections.text: More than 200 respiratory viruses can cause colds. Rhinoviruses are the most frequent cause of colds in the United States. Other respiratory viruses that can cause colds in the United States include common human coronaviruses, parainfluenza viruses, adenoviruses, enteroviruses (including EV-D68), and human metapneumovirus.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.text: SARS-CoV-2 (the virus that causes COVID-19), influenza virus (the virus that causes flu), and respiratory syncytial virus (the virus that causes RSV) can also cause cold-like symptoms but do not cause colds. These respiratory viruses are more likely to cause severe illness. Outcomes can include hospitalization or death, especially among groups at increased risk for severe illness. These include infants, older adults, or those with underlying medical conditions or weakened immune systems.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.text: If you have cold-like symptoms and suspect you have COVID-19 or flu, get tested, especially if you're at higher risk for severe illness. Antiviral treatments are available for COVID-19 and flu and work best when started very soon after symptoms begin.

sections.heading: Spread
sections.text: Different respiratory viruses spread in different ways. Most respiratory viruses are spread through droplets that an infected person releases when they cough or sneeze. These droplets can enter your body if you breathe them in or touch a contaminated surface and then touch your eyes, nose, or mouth. Some viruses can also spread through close personal contact, such as shaking hands with an infected person and then touching your eyes, nose, or mouth.

sections.heading: Spread
sections.text: You can get a cold any time of year. Many respiratory viruses, like influenza virus and RSV, usually circulate during winter, but other viruses that can also cause cold symptoms circulate during spring, summer, or fall.
